title: Love God, Serve Man -- Ch. 15: Peace is Everyone's Concern

primary_topics: Chapter 15 of 'Love God, Serve Man' -- CJP's speech of November 3, 1992 at the Hotel Inter-Continental before a joint meeting of the BBC, FINEX, MBC, MAP, PBSP and PCCI, arguing that peace is everyone's concern and that businessmen and professionals must help carry the Ramos government's Peace Process.

The role of the 'middle forces': as the 1986 EDSA revolution showed, non-violent revolutionary change requires 'an indispensable partnership between the peasant street marchers and the middle forces of business and the professions.'

His definition of true peace -- not the absence of violence, the victory of superior arms, or 'the eerie silence imposed by dictators and strong men,' but the resolution of the social, economic and political imbalances that cause armed conflict, so that peace, 'like justice,' means giving everyone his due.

Peace as requiring love as well as justice: since justice is 'impersonal and detached' and leaves the other 'another, or an alien,' genuine peace demands solidarity with the needy and a willingness to sacrifice private rights and possessions for the common good.
sub_topics: He opens with peace as the common cause of Christianity, Islam and Buddhism, the daily wish of the Mass -- 'Peace be with you' -- and the quest of every government, family and person, greeting his audience the same way.

He states the purpose of the gathering: for the country's leading business and professional groups to understand the Ramos government's Peace Process and, more importantly, to discuss what the 'middle forces' can and ought to do to hasten it.

He traces the middle class's peace effort to the first Multi-Sectoral Conference at the Asian Institute of Management on June 13, 1992, where the Workshop on Administration of Justice he chaired recommended -- and the conference endorsed -- the Peace Process as a priority of the first 100 days.

He credits the Ramos government with vigorously pursuing peace since then, and reports that at the second Multi-Sectoral Conference at De La Salle University on October 17, 1992 the peace process was hailed as among the administration's greatest achievements and endorsed for 'the next 1,000 days.'

He defines what peace is not -- mere absence of violence, victory of superior arms, or imposed silence -- and what it is: the resolution 'with sincerity and finality' of the imbalances that cause armed conflict, helping everyone 'to live with dignity and to enjoy the minimum necessities of human life.'

He gathers three authorities for that definition: Chief Justice Jose P. Laurel's 'humanization of all laws and the equalization of social and economic forces,' Pope John Paul I's solidarity of those who have more with those who have less, and PCP II's 'harmony in the human heart and in the social order.'

He argues that justice alone is insufficient because it is 'impersonal and detached,' leaving the other 'an alien,' whereas true peace, like love, makes the other 'a friend, even a brother or sister in the Lord.'

He makes peace the fruit of solidarity, possible only when the burning concern is not the assertion of legal rights or possessions but 'one's overpowering desire to share - out of love - with those who have no such legal rights or earthly possessions.'

He closes by calling the day historic, pledging 'a meaningful solidarity with the poor and the oppressed' and re-dedicating the resolve to rise from decades of conflict toward 'PEACE, JUSTICE and LOVE for all men in our "land of the morning."'

one_paragraph_summary: Chapter 15 of 'Love God, Serve Man' is CJP's November 3, 1992 speech at the Hotel Inter-Continental before a joint meeting of the Bishops-Businessmen's Conference, FINEX, the Makati Business Club, the Management Association of the Philippines, Philippine Business for Social Progress and the Philippine Chamber of Commerce and Industry, delivered while he served as the chamber's general counsel. He began from the premise that peace is everyone's concern -- espoused by Christianity, Islam and Buddhism alike, wished daily in every Mass, and sought by every government, family and person -- and greeted his audience with the same wish. The gathering's purpose, he said, was to make the country's leading business and professional groups aware of the Ramos government's Peace Process and to ask what the 'middle forces' could do to hasten it, since the 1986 EDSA revolution had shown that non-violent revolutionary change requires a partnership between street marchers and the middle class. He traced the private sector's peace effort to the first Multi-Sectoral Conference at the Asian Institute of Management in June 1992, where the Workshop on Administration of Justice he chaired recommended the Peace Process as a government priority, and to the second conference at De La Salle University that October, where it was hailed as a leading achievement and endorsed for the next 1,000 days. He then defined true peace negatively and positively: not the absence of violence, the victory of superior arms, or 'the eerie silence imposed by dictators and strong men,' but the resolution of the social, economic and political imbalances behind armed conflict -- Jose P. Laurel's humanization of laws and equalization of social and economic forces, John Paul I's solidarity of those who have more with those who have less, PCP II's harmony of heart and social order. Justice being impersonal, he argued, peace also requires love and sacrifice, and he closed pledging solidarity with the poor and re-dedicating the country to peace, justice and love.
